blocks.prompt: How a Grape Vine Climbs
blocks.text: A grape vine cannot stand up on its own. It has no trunk like a tree. Instead it grows long thin threads called tendrils. A tendril reaches out and feels around. When it touches a stick or a wire, it curls around and holds on tight. Then the vine pulls itself higher, toward the sun. The leaves catch the sunlight and turn it into sugar. The sugar travels down into the grapes. That is why a grape tastes sweet. It is full of sunshine that the leaves caught for it.

blocks.prompt: The Plant That Feels Its Way Up
blocks.text: A grape vine is a climber. It does not waste energy building a thick trunk. It borrows. Out of its stems grow tendrils, thin green threads that wave slowly through the air, searching. A tendril can feel. When its tip brushes against a branch or a wire, that touch sets off a change inside it. Within a few hours the tendril has wrapped itself around the support. Within a few days it has gone woody and hard, and now it grips like a fist. The vine hauls its leaves up into the light and leaves the hard work of standing to somebody else. Up in that light, the leaves do the real work. They pull in sunlight and air and build sugar. The sugar flows down the stems into the fruit. A green grape in early summer is hard and sour. Late in the season it softens, fills with sugar, and turns from green to gold or red or deep purple. Farmers call that turning point veraison. From then on, the grape is just getting sweeter and waiting.

notes: Vitis vinifera: the common grape vine

blocks.prompt: The Grape That Cannot Ripen Twice
blocks.text: Pick a banana too early and it will finish the job without you. Left on the counter, it turns from green to yellow to freckled brown, softening and sweetening the whole time. A grape will not do this. Once it is cut from the vine, a grape is finished. It will shrivel, it will spoil, but it will never get one bit sweeter. Scientists call fruits like this non-climacteric. Whatever sugar a grape has when the picker's hand closes around it is all the sugar it will ever have. That single fact runs the entire business. A grape farmer cannot pick early and hope. She has to walk the rows, taste, test, and decide, because the day she picks is the day the flavor is locked. Pick too early and the fruit stays sour forever. Pick too late and it turns soft and jammy. Sweetness begins at a moment called veraison. Before veraison the berry is small, hard, bright green, and full of acid, and it is busy growing. Then something switches. The berry stops growing and starts filling. Sugar pours in from the leaves. Color floods the skin, and the flesh goes soft enough to squeeze. Everything a grape is famous for happens after that switch, and all of it has to happen while the fruit is still attached to the plant. So the vine is not just a stand for the fruit. It is the factory. Cut the connection and production stops that second.

(inference: the vine makes the sugar and the fruit only stores it, so cutting the fruit off shuts production down)

notes: A fresh grape is about 80 percent water
A raisin is about 15 percent water

blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Preserves Itself
blocks.text: A fresh grape is about four fifths water. A raisin is about one seventh. Everything else about them is the same fruit. Nothing is added, nothing is cooked, and nothing is taken away except water, and that one subtraction turns a grape that spoils in a week into a raisin that keeps for a year. The reason is one of the oldest ideas in food. Mold and bacteria are living things, and living things need liquid water they can actually use. In a fresh grape, water moves freely, so a spore that lands on a bruise finds a swimming pool and a sugar supply. As the grape dries, the water leaves but the sugar stays, so the sugar that remains gets more and more concentrated. Sugar molecules hold water tightly to themselves. In a finished raisin there is still a little water, but almost none of it is free. A bacterium sitting on a raisin is surrounded by moisture it cannot drink. Food scientists call this water activity, and lowering it is why raisins, honey, jam, and dried meat all outlast the things they were made from. Doing this on purpose is simple and slow. In California's Central Valley, pickers lay bunches of grapes on paper trays on the ground between the vine rows in late August. The sun does the rest. Two or three weeks later the trays are rolled up and the raisins are shaken loose. It takes about four pounds of grapes to make one pound of raisins, which is why raisins have always cost more than they look like they should. The whole method rests on a gamble. Those grapes lie in the open, uncovered, for weeks. If it rains, the drying fruit soaks the water back up, splits, and molds, and a year of work rots on the ground in two days. Growers watch the September forecast the way other people watch a scoreboard. Ancient farmers worked all of this out without knowing any of the science. Dried grapes have been found in Egyptian tombs. Raisins traveled well, kept through winters, and packed more energy into less weight than almost anything else a person could carry. Long before refrigeration, a handful of shriveled grapes was one of the few ways to eat summer in the middle of winter.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Vitis vinifera, the European grape vine
Phylloxera: a root aphid from North America
Grafting: European tops on American roots
Grape varieties are clones, not families
Cultivated for around 8,000 years
Wild vines still grow near the Caspian Sea

blocks.prompt: Borrowed Roots
blocks.text: Consider what a seedless grape actually is. A seed is how a plant makes a new and different individual. It shuffles genes, and the offspring is not the parent. A grape with no seeds cannot do that. So how has the Thompson Seedless, the pale green grape in nearly every supermarket and inside most of the world's raisins, spread across millions of vines on several continents? It was cloned. Not in a laboratory, but in the oldest and simplest way there is. A grower cuts a length of woody stem from a vine, pushes it into damp soil, and it grows roots. The new plant is not a child of the old one. It is the old one, continued. Every Thompson Seedless vine alive today traces back by an unbroken chain of cuttings to a single vine, and that vine to a single ancient mutation. The variety does not have a family tree. It has a length. This is why grape varieties are so old. Pinot Noir has been recognizably itself for more than six hundred years. When you eat a grape of a named variety, you are eating fruit from a plant that is, genetically, the same individual that some farmer decided was worth keeping, centuries ago and a world away. Vineyards are less like farms than like museums that happen to be alive. The strategy has an obvious weakness, and in the nineteenth century the weakness arrived. In 1863, vines in southern France began to die for no visible reason. Leaves yellowed, wood withered, whole hillsides emptied. The cause was found underground: phylloxera, a root-feeding aphid no bigger than a pinhead, imported by accident from North America on collected vines. In North America it was harmless. Wild American grape species had spent millions of years alongside it and carried roots that resisted it. The European wine grape, Vitis vinifera, had no such history and no such roots. Cloned endlessly from a narrow set of ancestors, Europe's vineyards were not a population of individuals. They were one target repeated a million times. Phylloxera destroyed roughly two thirds of France's vineyards within about thirty years, then swept on through Spain, Italy, and eventually most of the wine-growing world. The French government offered an enormous prize for a cure. Growers flooded fields where the land was flat enough to hold water, buried live toads beneath the vines, poured chemicals into the soil. The insect kept eating. The solution, championed by the French botanist Jules Emile Planchon with help from the American entomologist Charles Valentine Riley, was to accept the loss and cheat. If American roots resisted phylloxera and European fruit was what people wanted, then join the two. Cut a shoot of vinifera, splice it onto American rootstock, and let the wound heal into one working plant. Europe above the graft, America below it. Growers hated the idea. It sounded like surrender, and many were certain the fruit would taste of the foreign roots. It did not, and it remains the only reliable answer. Nearly every wine grape and table grape grown today, in France, Italy, Spain, and California alike, is a European vine standing on American roots. A few isolated pockets, protected by sandy soil or sheer distance, still grow vines on their own roots, and they are treated as precious oddities. Look at the base of any grafted vine and you will find the seam where the two were joined. So a bunch of grapes is stranger than it looks. The fruit is a clone with no family tree, kept alive by cutting. The roots holding it up belong to a different species from a different continent, chosen because it survived a war the top half could not fight. Nothing about it is natural in any simple sense, and none of it would exist without a very long argument between people and a plant.
